Kidneys
KID-neez
n. pl.
Middle English kidenei, of uncertain formation. Webster 1828: the two glandular bodies in the lower part of the abdomen which secrete the urine. In the Authorized Version the word belongs almost entirely to the sacrificial law — the two kidneys with their fat are burned upon the altar — and once, figuratively, to the richest part of the wheat.

Biblical Definition

The kidneys are what God claims from the inside of the animal. The formula runs unchanged through Leviticus: And the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away (Leviticus 3:4), and again at Leviticus 4:9, and again at Leviticus 7:4. When the priests were consecrated the same parts were taken: the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys, and their fat, and Moses burned it upon the altar (Leviticus 8:16). What is burned is the deepest and richest interior of the sacrifice, the part no worshipper sees and no one eats. That is the doctrine. God is not satisfied with the visible surrender; He requires what is hidden. Scripture elsewhere uses the kidneys (rendered reins in the KJV) for the inmost self that God alone examines. The figure runs the other way too: Israel is fed with the fat of kidneys of wheat (Deuteronomy 32:14), the choicest of the grain. And in judgment the sword of the LORD is made fat with fatness… with the fat of the kidneys of rams (Isaiah 34:6), the sacrificial vocabulary turned against a nation that would not sacrifice.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines KIDNEY as one of the two glandular bodies which secrete the urine, and notes the figurative English use for sort or temperament. The biblical use is sacrificial and, through the KJV’s reins, moral: the hidden inward parts.

expand to see more

KIDNEY, n. — The kidneys are two glandular bodies, situated in the lower part of the abdomen, one on each side, whose office is to secrete the urine.

Also used figuratively in English for sort, kind, or temperament — a man of that kidney.

The Authorized Version renders the same Hebrew word reins when the sense is moral rather than anatomical, as in the LORD trieth the hearts and reins — which keeps Webster’s two senses joined: the innermost organ, and the innermost man.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 3:4 — "And the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away."

Leviticus 4:9 — "And the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away,"

Leviticus 8:16 — "And he took all the fat that was upon the inwards, and the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys, and their fat, and Moses burned it upon the altar."

Deuteronomy 32:14 — "Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, with fat of lambs, and rams of the breed of Bashan, and goats, with the fat of kidneys of wheat; and thou didst drink the pure blood of the grape."

Isaiah 34:6 — "The sword of the LORD is filled with blood, it is made fat with fatness, and with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams: for the LORD hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure here is squeamishness — the modern instinct to skip Leviticus as primitive butchery — and the loss of the doctrine that God claims the hidden interior and not the presentable exterior.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No movement is redefining the kidneys. What is happening is quieter: whole congregations have never heard Leviticus read, and preachers who do read it hurry past the anatomy as though it were an embarrassment inherited from a cruder age. The repetition is deliberate. Four times in four chapters the same interior parts are named, and the effect on a reader who does not skip is cumulative — God specified what He would have burned, down to the fat beside the flanks.

The principle to recover is that God requires the inward parts. The same Hebrew word the sacrificial law uses for the kidneys the psalmists use for the seat of the affections, which the KJV renders reins: Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart (Psalm 26:2). A religion of surfaces has always been available, and Leviticus 3 forecloses it. If the altar took the kidneys and the caul, then the God of the altar is not content with the parts of a man that show.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew noun is kilyah, the kidneys; the KJV renders it kidneys in sacrificial contexts and reins where the sense is the inmost self. It is the standard Old Testament figure for what only God can examine.

expand to see more

Hebrew kilyah (H3629) — kidneys; used of the sacrificial portions (Leviticus 3:4; 4:9; 8:16) and figuratively of the innermost man.

The KJV translates the same word reins at Psalm 7:9, Psalm 26:2, and Jeremiah 11:20 — the LORD trieth the hearts and reins.

Hebrew cheleb (H2459) — the fat; forbidden as food (Leviticus 3:17) because it is the LORD’s portion on the altar.

The figurative fat of kidneys of wheat (Deuteronomy 32:14) transfers the sacrificial vocabulary of richness to the harvest.

Greek nephros (G3510) carries the same double sense into Revelation 2:23, he which searcheth the reins and hearts.

Usage

"The two kidneys, and the fat that is on them (Leviticus 3:4) — the formula of the peace offering, repeated without variation."

"The fat of kidneys of wheat (Deuteronomy 32:14) — the richest of the grain, described in sacrificial terms."

"The fat of the kidneys of rams (Isaiah 34:6) — the language of the altar turned into the language of judgment."
